title: The Dashboard Delusion
author: Managing the Future
summary: An experienced CEO deconstructs the persistent fantasy of the 'God system' — the belief that if only the right information architecture existed (ERP in the 1990s, dashboards in the 2000s, AI now), a CEO could achieve near-omniscience and make near-perfect decisions. The article argues that this fantasy reveals a fundamental misunderstanding of what running a company actually is: not an information problem but a judgment problem. Every data point in a CEO's dashboard describes decisions that have already been made; it cannot tell you whether those decisions were in the right direction, whether the strategy is right, whether you have the right people in the right roles, or whether the culture is actually performing. The CEO's most important questions — What is our vision? Is our strategy right? Do we have the right people? Is the culture working? — are all beyond what data can answer. The article is a sharp warning for leaders currently tempted to invest in AI-powered decision support systems as a substitute for the judgment, presence, and alignment work that is the real substance of senior leadership.
points: Every number in a dashboard describes the past: decisions already made, directions already taken, culture already established — data is a record, not a map.

The CEO's highest-leverage questions — vision, strategy, people quality, culture health — are precisely the questions that data cannot answer, because they concern conditions and judgments that have no data counterpart yet.

AI will be able to perform the 'information aggregation and analysis' function of CEOs better than humans can, which is why leaders who define their role as information processors are, in the author's framing, replaceable.

What makes senior leadership irreplaceable is the judgment work: reading what a person can do two roles larger than their current one, sensing whether a strategy is alive or stale, knowing whether the culture is actually performing or just looking good on engagement surveys.

The 'God system' pursuit is a time-allocation problem: senior leaders who chase comprehensive dashboards are spending their scarcest resource — time — on the wrong thing, because the returns on data aggregation are lower than the returns on the alignment and judgment work only they can do.
quotes: And for as long as I can remember, CEOs have been looking for what I call the “God system.” This system would gather all the data about everything happening in the company, then present it in a way that lets the CEO make informed, near-perfect decisions. The new God system was a single view of all company analytics—revenue, pipeline, margin, hiring, churn, engagement.

Because in the future, AI will perform this exercise far better than any human ever could. If you are still chasing the fantasy of a God system for the CEO, you fundamentally view running the company as an information problem.
What it doesn’t tell you is: Are they running in the right direction? Are they making decisions aligned with your vision and strategy for the company?

Strategy is a hypothesis about how this company will win in a market that has not finished revealing itself. You can test pieces of it against evidence, but the bet itself is an act of judgment about conditions that have not occurred.

The answers are not in the data, because the answers are about the future that has to be chosen and created. Obsessive measuring of the past, and even the making of predictions based primarily on analysis of historical data, will not help you steer ahead.

But the knowledge required to make those thousands of decisions well is not at the center and never will be. He writes in part: Leadership is about making only the choices that you are best positioned to make — and not making the ones for which you aren’t, even if you are more senior than the person who will make the choice.

The job is to build a company in which thousands of distributed decisions get made well, in alignment, by the people closest to the facts. What AI actually changes All this said, I am an optimist about AI in the enterprise.
